Class Flow

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.AbstractPanelElement
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.Flow
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
public final class Flow extends AbstractPanelElement
A run of elements laid out left to right at the panel's runtime width, wrapping onto new rows when it runs out of room: the runtime row. Holds heterogeneous children (buttons, checkboxes, labels, icons), the element analog of SlotFlowElement. 
Flow.builder().gap(10, 4)
        .add(onOffToggle)
        .add(Flow.spacer())
        .add(resetButton)            // pinned to the right edge
        .build();

Spacers: label left, control right

spacer() is a gap that takes whatever the row's other children and gaps leave of the Flow's width, split evenly among the row's spacers (the odd pixel to the last). The Flow's gap sits only between two pieces of content; a spacer adds its share and never a gap of its own, so a row's natural width and its layout count the same pixels wherever the spacer sits. A row with a spacer therefore fills the Flow's width: a label, a spacer and a control is a settings row with the control pinned to the right edge, at whatever width the panel has, with no width handed to whoever built it (a Tabs body factory never knows its width). A spacer at each end of a one-row Flow centers what is between them. When the row is too narrow and wraps, a spacer that ends up at the start or end of a row takes nothing, and the control sits under its label.

Vertical alignment in a row (7.3.0)

A row top-aligns its children by default. Flow.Builder.crossAlign with CrossAlign.CENTER centers each child on its row's line instead, and CrossAlign.END sets it on the line's bottom, so a label beside a 20 px control, or a mod's toggle beside a list's 16 px buttons, sit level with no pixel offsets. The line is the tallest child's first line: a child that grew past its baseline (an open Section, a wrapped label) aligns by its baseline and grows downward, so its header stays on the line. 
Flow.builder().crossAlign(CrossAlign.CENTER)
        .add(nameLabel)                  // centered on the toggle's height
        .add(Flow.spacer())
        .add(toggle)
        .build();

Reactive sizing

naturalWidth() is every child side by side, so the panel hands the Flow the room it has; each layout pass lays the children out to that width (a label too long for the row wraps, a button caps), wraps them into rows, and reports the hug of the result (getWidth()/getHeight(); the full width when a row has a spacer). A wrap reports its extra rows as extraLayoutHeight(), so the panel pushes what is below down.

Vertical: a column that wraps into columns

Flow.Builder.vertical() turns the Flow on its side: children fill top to bottom and, when the next one would pass the wrap height, start a new column to the right. The wrap height is the room from the Flow's top edge down to where the frame beside its panel ends (wrapHeight(int)): the panel learns it from its host, the way a filling element learns its height from its panel. So a column of switches beside the player inventory wraps into a second column at the bottom of the container screen's frame. With no frame beside the panel (a HUD panel, a panel above or below the frame, a pixel-placed one) the Flow is one column. The Flow's width is its columns side by side, so its panel grows with each column and a RIGHT_* region still places it beside the frame. 
Flow.builder().vertical().gap(1)
        .add(settingsButton)
        .add(lockSwitch)
        .add(restockSwitch)           // ... a second column once the frame ends
        .build();
In a vertical Flow gap(horizontal, vertical) is the gap between columns and the gap between children in a column; a spacer takes no room.

At most so many in a column (7.5.0)

Flow.Builder.wrapAfter caps how many shown children a column holds (a row, in a row Flow), whatever room is left: a column that would overlap something past two slots wraps after two. The cap is read every frame, so it can follow the game mode or a setting. A column fills from its first child, so the latest ones wrap out; with Flow.Builder.keepLast() the last ones keep the first column and the earliest step out into the next, to its right: 
Flow.builder().vertical().gap(0).wrapAfter(2).keepLast()
        .add(enderSlot)               // steps out, right of the elytra
        .add(elytraSlot)
        .add(totemSlot)               // elytra and totem keep the first column
        .build();
With two shown, that is one column with the ender slot on top, as without the cap.

A filling child (7.3.0)

In a vertical Flow a child that fills (ScrollContainer.builder().fillHeight()) gets the height the Flow is given less its other children and gaps, so a header and a "New" row sit above a list that takes the rest and scrolls by itself. Such a Flow fills too, and does not wrap into columns.

Hidden children

Either way a hidden child takes no room: the next one moves up into its place, so the Flow reflows when a child hides or shows.

An interactive host

The children live inside the Flow, which places them itself (in the panel's content coordinates, so they share its origin). Render and input reach them through ChildDispatch, exactly as the same elements directly on the panel: clicks, the wheel, keys, releases, popovers, attach and detach. A disabled Flow (its own disabledWhen) disables everything in it.

Boxed: a card

Flow.Builder.boxed() draws a card behind the children: a row of a list that reads as one unit (a world in a world list). The children sit BOX_PADDING inside the card's edge, a boxed row Flow fills the width its panel gives it, and its height hugs its rows plus the padding. The card's look follows the kind of screen: in the Default look a dark translucent box with a one-pixel light border that brightens while hovered, in the Panel look the INSET panel style. An icon beside a stack of lines is a boxed Flow holding the icon and a vertical Flow: 
Flow.builder().boxed().gap(6)
        .add(icon)
        .add(Flow.builder().vertical().gap(2)
                .add(title).add(detail).add(buttonRow).build())
        .build();

    • extraLayoutHeight

      public int extraLayoutHeight()
      The extra height of the rows past the first: what a wrap adds. A child that grew past its own baseline (an open Section, a wrapped label, a ListView, whose baseline is nothing) counts at its baseline (7.3.0), so its growth is the Flow's too and what is below is pushed down by it; a list row's controls stay centered on the row's first line. In a row Flow a vertical Flow child counts whole: what it reports is its stack, not growth. A vertical Flow's own extra is its stack past its tallest child's baseline, which stays put as its children grow, so a list in a column pushes what is below the column.

    • renderCulled

      public void renderCulled(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Called each frame instead of PanelElement.render(RenderContext) for a visible element that is skipped only because its box lies wholly outside the clip in play (7.4.0): a row scrolled out of a ScrollContainer, a list's row past its scroll area, a section of the container region out of view. The element is still shown, just not on screen, so it can mark its state as held rather than gone: a slot element keeps its slot parked instead of handing it back to the menu's layout, as it would for a hidden one. Never called for a hidden element (its own PanelElement.isVisible() false, or a hidden or collapsed parent): that one gets neither call.

      An element that contains others forwards it to its shown children (ChildDispatch.renderCulled(List, RenderContext)), so a culled section reaches the slots inside it. The context is the one PanelElement.render(RenderContext) would have had. Default: no-op.

    • renderOverlay

      public void renderOverlay(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Second-pass render for transient overlays that draw outside the element's layout bounds (a Dropdown's popover). Runs after every element's PanelElement.render(RenderContext), so an overlay is always on top regardless of declaration order. Pairs with PanelElement.getActiveOverlayBounds(InputContext), the input side. Default: no-op.

    • getActiveOverlayBounds

      public int @Nullable [] getActiveOverlayBounds(InputContext in)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      The screen-space bounds [x, y, width, height] of this element's active overlay (an open popover), or null when none is open.     • notifyClickOutsideOverlay

      public void notifyClickOutsideOverlay(InputContext in)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Tells an element with transient open state (a popover) that a click landed somewhere it did not claim, so it can close. The dispatchers call it on every shown element for every click, even one another element consumed; each element decides for itself whether the click was outside. Default: no-op.

    • screenKind

      public void screenKind(ScreenKind kind)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      The kind of screen the owning panel is on, handed down whenever it changes, before the next layout pass. For an element whose size depends on the kind (a Tabs insets its body on a Default-look screen's page), so it measures for the screen it is on from the first frame. An element holding others passes it on to them (a ScrollContainer in a Tabs body sizes its band's inset by it). Default: no-op.

    • inDialog

      public void inDialog(boolean inDialog)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Whether the owning panel is a dialog (a modal, Panel.tracksAsModal) rather than part of the screen, handed down when that is set (7.2.0). On an Default-look screen a list band (a ScrollContainer's, a Tabs page) insets its content by the full screen's ScrollContainer.DEFAULT_INSET_X and ScrollContainer.DEFAULT_INSET_Y; inside a dialog the frame and its padding are already the margin, so a band insets by the dialog's own gap, ScrollContainer.DIALOG_INSET, instead. An element holding others passes it on to them. Default: no-op.

    • inBand

      public void inBand(boolean inBand)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Whether the element sits on a list band another element draws (7.3.0): a Tabs page whose body fills it (PanelElement.fillHeight(int)). There a ScrollContainer draws no band of its own (no second background, no separators, no second inset), only its scrollbar, so the page looks the same whichever side scrolls. Handed down before layout; an element holding others passes it on to them. Default: no-op.
